name: Asian Ginseng
summary: A root long used in traditional Chinese medicine as a calming adaptogen, now widely marketed for cognitive function, fatigue, and blood sugar support.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH reports small studies suggest possible improvements in abstract thinking, attention, and reaction time in middle-aged adults, but not in young adults, and memory benefits appeared to depend on combining it with ginkgo rather than ginseng alone.

A 2023 review of 19 studies covering over 2,400 participants found some support for reducing fatigue, but mainly when ginseng was combined with other ingredients rather than used alone, and results were mixed across the body of research.
NCCIH states the majority of research shows Asian ginseng does not improve athletic performance.

safetyNotes.text: Insomnia is the most commonly reported side effect.
May interfere with blood clotting and may lower blood sugar levels; talk to a provider before combining with blood-thinning or diabetes medication.
May worsen autoimmune disorders. Not recommended during pregnancy.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Cat's Claw
summary: A woody vine from the Amazon rainforest used traditionally to help ward off illness, now marketed for joint conditions and immune support.

claims.useCase: Osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis joint symptoms
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH states there is no conclusive evidence from human studies supporting cat's claw for any health purpose; existing human studies generally have weak methodology and small sample sizes, so no firm conclusion can be drawn for joint conditions specifically.

safetyNotes.text: May stimulate immune system activity, which could worsen symptoms in people with autoimmune conditions — check with a provider first.
May slow blood clotting; talk to a provider before combining with blood-thinning medication.
Research suggests use during pregnancy may be unsafe.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Chamomile
summary: A daisy-like flower traditionally taken as a tea, long explored for calming and digestive support.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH notes some small studies suggest chamomile may help with mild generalized anxiety, but overall evidence is limited and not conclusive.
Traditional use is well documented, but rigorous clinical evidence specific to digestive complaints is limited per NCCIH.

safetyNotes.text: People allergic to ragweed, daisies, marigolds, or chrysanthemums may also react to chamomile.
May increase the effect of blood-thinning medication.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Cranberry
summary: A tart fruit long used by Native Americans and settlers, most commonly explored today as a way to help reduce the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections.

claims.useCase: Reducing risk of recurrent urinary tract infections
claims.gradeRationale: Cranberry products appear to reduce the risk of symptomatic, recurrent UTIs in women by roughly 25% in some analyses, but results are inconsistent across studies. The FDA permits a qualified claim describing the evidence as 'limited' (or 'limited and inconsistent' for juice products). Cranberry is not a treatment for an active infection — only a possible preventive measure.

safetyNotes.text: Large quantities may cause stomach upset or diarrhea, especially in young children.
If you have symptoms of a urinary tract infection, see a healthcare provider for proper evaluation rather than relying on cranberry alone.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Ginkgo
summary: A tree native to China whose leaf extract is among the most-studied herbal supplements, traditionally explored for memory support and circulation.

claims.useCase: Supporting memory or cognitive function in age-related decline
claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH reports that overall scientific evidence does not support ginkgo for preventing or slowing cognitive decline; some individual trials show modest effects but results are inconsistent across the body of evidence.
NCCIH notes evidence does not support ginkgo as an effective treatment for tinnitus.

safetyNotes.text: May increase bleeding risk, particularly when combined with blood-thinning medication.
Raw or roasted ginkgo seeds are toxic and are not the same product as standardized leaf-extract supplements.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Goldenseal
summary: A woodland plant used traditionally by Native Americans for digestive complaints and wound care, now commonly marketed for colds and respiratory infections.

claims.useCase: Colds, respiratory infections, or digestive complaints
claims.gradeRationale: Traditional use is long documented, but NCCIH states there isn't enough reliable research from rigorous human studies to say whether goldenseal helps with any health condition. Berberine, a compound in goldenseal, has been studied for blood sugar and cholesterol effects, but very little is absorbed when goldenseal itself is taken orally, so those findings may not carry over.

safetyNotes.text: Some commercial goldenseal products have been found to contain undisclosed or substituted ingredients.
Not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or for infants — its berberine content can be harmful to newborns.
May alter how the body processes other medications; talk to a provider before combining with any medicine, especially diabetes medication like metformin.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: Green Tea
summary: A minimally-processed tea leaf used for thousands of years, widely studied today for cholesterol, weight, and heart health, alongside one FDA-approved topical use.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH reports green tea modestly lowered total and LDL cholesterol across studies, though it showed no effect on HDL cholesterol or triglycerides.

NCCIH notes catechins and caffeine in green tea may have a modest effect on body weight, but results vary by product and individual, and most trials tested concentrated extract supplements rather than the beverage.

safetyNotes.text: Concentrated tablet or capsule extracts have rarely been linked to liver injury; the brewed beverage has no such reports. People with a certain genetic variant, present in an estimated 5-15% of Americans, may be more susceptible.
Contains caffeine; extract supplements can cause nausea, constipation, abdominal discomfort, or increased blood pressure.
May reduce blood levels of some medications, including the beta-blocker nadolol, the cholesterol medication atorvastatin, and the osteoporosis medication raloxifene.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. See the full disclaimer for details.

name: St. John's Wort
summary: A flowering plant traditionally explored for mood support. One of the herbs with the best-documented drug interactions of any botanical supplement.

claims.gradeRationale: NCCIH reports that some studies suggest St. John's wort may be of benefit for mild to moderate depression, though findings are mixed across trials and it is not established as effective for major depression.

safetyNotes.text: Interacts with a large number of prescription medications by speeding up how the body breaks them down, which can make those medications less effective. See the interaction checker before combining with any medication.
Can increase sensitivity to sunlight.

disclaimerShort: Traditional/supplement use only, not a substitute for medical advice. This herb has significant drug interactions — see the full disclaimer.
